study.title: Mark 11 The King's Entry, the Judgment on Sterility and the Confrontation of Authority
study.overview: Mark 11 marks the arrival of Jesus at the centre of Israel's religious life and shows, in sequence, his entry into Jerusalem, the symbolic judgment on the fig tree, the purification of the temple and direct confrontation with the Jewish leaders. The chapter unites messianic acclaim and conflict: the same Jesus who is received with hosanas also exposes a religion without fruit, without true prayer and without recognition of God's authority. The text presents the royalty of Jesus, his freedom before the opponents, his zeal for the house of God and the growing blindness of the leaders who question him.

outline.title: Messianic entrance to Jerusalem
outline.explanation: Jesus deliberately enters the city in a picture of popular acclaim. The colt, the clothes on the way and the cries of praise signal that he comes as the expected King, although his royalty appears in humility and not in ostentation. At the end of the scene, he examines the temple and returns to Bethany, indicating that his visit to the city has a spiritual and not just political focus.

outline.title: The fruitless fig tree and the purification of the temple
outline.explanation: The next day, Jesus seeks fruit in a showy fig tree, but finds only leaves; the act becomes a sign of what happens in the temple. He expels sellers and buyers, interrupts the profane use of sacred space and cites the Scriptures to denounce that the house of prayer for the nations was transformed into a den of thieves. The reaction of the religious leaders shows that the crisis is now open and that their opposition has already become a murderer.

outline.title: Dry fig tree, faith and forgiveness
outline.explanation: The dry fig tree confirms the prophetic meaning of the previous gesture. Jesus guides the disciples to have faith in God, speaks about confident prayer and connects the life of prayer to forgiveness granted to others. Thus, trust in God is not religious magic; it comes accompanied by a correct relationship with others and the heavenly Father.

outline.title: Authority of Jesus and the refusal of leaders
outline.explanation: The leaders ask where the authority of Jesus comes from, but he answers with another question about John's baptism. They are unable to respond with sincerity, imprisoned to the fear of the people and to political calculus. By saying that they do not know, reveal their moral blindness and lose the opportunity to recognize the divine origin of the ministry of John and Jesus.

study.context: The chapter is set in the last week of Jesus before the crucifixion. The biblical text places the movement between Bethany, the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem and the temple. The notes provided highlight that Mark organizes these events as part of Jesus" great confrontation with the temple and the leaders of Jerusalem. It is also observed that Jesus spends the night in Bethany and returns in the morning to ministerial work in Jerusalem. The text does not require additional conjectures beyond these indications.
study.theology: Mark 11 presents Jesus as the Messianic King who enters Jerusalem with authority, but also as the holy judge who examines the worship of Israel. The collar and the hosanas point to Messianic fulfillment and recognition, but popular reception does not avoid judgment on spiritual sterility. The fig tree works as a visible sign of an invisible reality: fruitless life appearance. The temple, the center of religious life, is valued in the light of God's purpose - house of prayer for all nations - and not simply as an institutional space. Prayer, in turn, is treated as real trust in God, inseparable for forgiveness. Finally, the question about authority shows that the problem of leaders is not a lack of information, but hardness of heart and refusal to submit to the truth already revealed in John and Jesus.

scholarViews.insight: The response of the leaders, "we do not know," shows his inability to answer a simple question and reveals his blindness and hostility, which causes them to lose their religious legitimacy at this point.
The public entrance of Jesus to Jerusalem shows that he does not hide from the enemies nor is he slain in the face of the coming suffering.
Jesus examines everything in the temple before leaving, indicating a thorough assessment of the order of worship and the condition of the sacred place.

questions: What does the acclaim of Jesus as King teach us about the difference between religious enthusiasm and true discipleship?
How does the fruitless fig tree confront the appearance of spirituality without real obedience?
How does the connection between prayer and forgiveness correct the idea that faith is just asking God?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to examine whether his life has only leaves or also fruit. In practice, this means approaching Christ with real submission, reviewing the quality of personal and community worship, abandoning any form of empty religiosity and cultivating prayer marked by trust and forgiveness. He also calls us not to answer with evasive when God has already spoken clearly: honesty before the truth is part of fidelity. A concrete application is to separate time this week to pray, to ask God to reveal areas of spiritual sterility and then to reconcile with someone to whom you keep resentment.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not explain in detail whether the fig tree and temple should be read only as prophetic signs or also as a direct announcement of the judgment on Jerusalem in the historical sense; the above interpretation follows the line of notes, without stating more than they support. There is also no basis for the sources provided to broaden the discussion about dates, geography beyond the text, or a more specific historical context than the last week of Jesus in Jerusalem.
